lesson.title: Reading the Margins: One Variable at a Time
lesson.summary: A marginal distribution describes a single variable from a two-way table by using its row or column totals, ignoring the other variable entirely.
lesson.body:
The word marginal sounds technical, but it describes something almost literal: a marginal distribution is read straight from the margins, the row totals and column totals, of a two-way table. If you covered up the interior cells of the students' phone-and-grade table and looked only at the totals running along the edges, you would still be able to describe each variable completely on its own. That is exactly what a marginal distribution is, and the name simply reflects where the numbers physically sit on the page.

Formally, the marginal distribution of a variable is the distribution of that variable alone, found by taking each of its category totals and dividing by the grand total, ignoring the second variable completely. It can be reported as counts, straight from the margin, or as percentages of the whole sample, which is usually more useful for comparing groups of different sizes. Either way, you are describing one variable exactly as if the two-way table had never mentioned a second variable at all, which means a marginal distribution could just as easily be graphed with an ordinary bar graph or pie chart, the same tools you would use for any single categorical variable.

Using the earlier table of 300 students, where the column totals are 160 iPhone users and 140 Android users, and the row totals are 120 freshmen and 180 sophomores, the marginal distribution of operating system is 160 divided by 300, or about 53.3 percent iPhone, and 140 divided by 300, or about 46.7 percent Android. Those two percentages add to 100 percent, as they must, since every student in the survey uses exactly one of the two operating systems. Separately, the marginal distribution of grade level is 120 divided by 300, or 40 percent freshmen, and 180 divided by 300, or 60 percent sophomores, which also add to 100 percent. Notice that each marginal distribution is computed from a different set of totals, the column totals for operating system and the row totals for grade level, but both divide by the same grand total of 300.

Notice that computing a marginal distribution never touches the interior cells of the table, only the totals. That means a marginal distribution cannot tell you anything about how the two variables relate to each other; it treats them as if they were reported separately. Knowing that 53.3 percent of the whole sample uses an iPhone says nothing about whether freshmen and sophomores use iPhones at similar rates or very different rates, and two very different tables of interior cell counts could easily produce the exact same pair of marginal distributions.

To see whether the two variables actually relate to each other, whether being a freshman changes the chance of owning an iPhone, you need to look inside a single row or column rather than at the whole table. That narrower view, the distribution of one variable restricted to one category of the other, is exactly what a conditional distribution provides, and it is where the real relationship between two categorical variables becomes visible.
